name: Black Shadows
lede: Black Shadows is a pale greyish pink in our data, which is a good reason to look at what painters learned about shadows: they are rarely black.

sections.title: A name that points to a painting lesson
sections.body:
The swatch #BFAFB2 is a light, soft grey-pink and is nothing like black [1]. The books we have read give no history for the name itself, only for the idea inside it [1].

Ball describes Rembrandt's deep shadows as glazes of bone black, red lake and red ochre, so dark that the wall is hardly distinguishable from black shadow [2]. In contrast, he reports Renoir's saying that no shadow is black and that it always has a colour [3]. Impressionist shadows, Ball adds, were not dark but infused with colour [3].

Gurney makes a related point about night scenes: a painter shows what the eye sees, whereas a camera records a lot of black shadows [4].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of 23,781 paintings, 125 match this color, 0.53%, as photographed [1]. It peaks in the 1900s at 2.4 times the expected rate, and inside a painting it most often plays a light [1]. The name is first recorded in 1912 in Ridgway [1]. John Singer Sargent paints it most often, in 4 of 287 works, but no painter stands out against the museum baseline [1].
